projectDesc.p: The Middle English Texts Series offers a diverse and representative array of literary texts that medieval readers in the present-day British Isles would have encountered between the twelfth and sixteenth centuries. It is committed to making available both affordable print and open access editions to scholars, teachers, and students of the Western Middle Ages. In its digital publications, the series prioritizes a user-friendly interface and viewing options, multiple downloadable formats, enhanced searchability and filtering, and accessibility to the widest possible range of users.

editorialDecl.p: METS takes as its mission the creation of affordable editions that would pass scrutiny from the most demanding expert, yet would prove comprehensible, and even enticing, to someone who had never read Middle English before. This agenda dictates that METS publications offer not a critical edition reflecting all surviving manuscripts, and certainly not a diplomatic edition, but a best-text edition, informed by the notes and apparatus of earlier editions (where these exist), and by substantive variants from other manuscript witnesses. Transcriptions of Middle English texts are lightly modernized to ensure a smooth reading experience, while non-English texts preserve both the original language and a modern English translation in facing-page format. Each edition offers expert assistance with language and lexicon, providing glosses alongside the text(s), textual and explanatory notes, elucidation of unfamiliar contexts and traditions, and thematic and interpretive possibilities. All editions feature general introductions that set the edited text within its own time, place, and traditions, and link it to ancestor, congener, and successor materials. All publications contain comprehensive, current bibliographies of pertinent scholarship and criticism. House style is adapted from the Chicago Manual of Style.

correction.p: This text may include corrections made after the original edition went to press in order to correct errors and improve glosses. For a full list of editorial and typographical corrections made to this edition, please view its correction log on Github: https://github.com/mets-editions/douma-ashby/blob/main/douma-ashby-export-corrections-log.xlsx

div.p: All translations in the notes, unless otherwise specified, are mine.

note.p: Margarete, dei gratia regine Anglie. Ashby was employed as Queen Margaret’s signet clerk from around the time of her marriage to Henry VI in 1445 until the exile of the Lancastrian royal family in 1461. Sebastian Sobecki interprets Ashby’s choice of the word “nuper” (lately) as evidence for a composition date of the poem shortly after the end of Ashby’s employment as signet clerk in 1461. See Sobecki-Words, p. 185.

numquam tota vita sua in alio servicio. Before being employed in the royal household, Ashby served as clerk in the household of Humphrey, Duke of Gloucester, where he also received his education. As the uncle of King Henry VI and the Lord Protector of the Realm following Henry V’s death, Gloucester was one of the most powerful noblemen during Henry VI’s minority and a figurehead of the Lancastrian family. In the 1440s, Gloucester fell from grace and retired from public life. By claiming that he never worked for anyone except for the prince’s “noble blood” (“nobilem sanguinem”), Ashby positions himself as a Lancastrian man, without explicitly associating himself with the disgraced duke.

div.note:
1
O maisters Gower, Chaucer, and Lydgate. Ashby opens his poem by invoking three of his famous poetic predecessors, John Gower (d. 1408), Geoffrey Chaucer (d. 1400), and John Lydgate (d. 1451), as the triumvirate of English poetry. He was not the first to do so: Osbert Bokenham had also included these three poets in the opening invocation of a poem in 1447, though Ashby is unlikely to have been familiar with this work (Meyer-Lee, “Laureates and Beggars,” pp. 714–15). His choice for these three poets, and in particular his choice to include John Lydgate rather than Thomas Hoccleve, whose work Ashby must have known, was probably influenced by his desire to establish himself as the heir of their recognized poetic authority. Much more than Hoccleve, as Robert Meyer-Lee argues, Lydgate was a poet laureate with an authority that was seen to be independent from royal power. As such, through this triumvirate Ashby “constructs a legitimate and unmistakably Lancastrian poetic heritage, the authority of which [. . .] finds its present embodiment in himself” (Meyer-Lee, “Laureates and Beggars,” p. 715). See also Mortimer, John Lydgate’s Fall of Princes, pp. 1–24, for a discusison of the triumvirate of Chaucer, Gower, and Lydgate in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries.

22
So I, George Asshby. Unlike the writers of the many medieval texts and poems that have come down to us as anonymous, Ashby explicitly inscribes his identity in the text, both in the Latin prose (¶1) and in the Middle English verse. Thus, the reader is continually reminded of the poet’s historical identity as signet clerk of the Lancastrian royal family.

28
Not as a maister, but as a pentise. The humility topos is a common trope in many later Middle English poems. The writer downplays his own poetic abilities, humbling himself before the examples of his predecessors — the great predecessor usually being Geoffrey Chaucer. A striking example of this trope is found in Thomas Hoccleve’s Regiment of Princes: “Symple is my goost and scars my letterure [. . .] And fadir, Chaucer, fayn wolde han me taght, / But I was dul and lerned lyte or naght” (ed. Blyth, lines 2073, 2078–79). Later critics have often taken the humility topos rather literally, as evidence that fifteenth-century poetry was not as accomplished as that of earlier centuries. However, in his influential 1987 article, David Lawton has convincingly shown such humility claims to be clever strategies to disavow responsibility for the potentially offensive content of the poem. See Lawton, “Dullness and the Fifteenth Century,” which discusses both the example from Hoccleve quoted above and these lines from Ashby’s Active Policy and Dicta.

51
Of many bookes right sentenciall. Ashby’s claim to not have read many books or scripture is, as Meyer-Lee has also noted, belied by his inclusion of many quotations from Latin sources in the Active Policy and Dicta. As Meyer-Lee observes, the Dicta forms an “implicit counterclaim” to these lines by showing Ashby to be “no mere scribe, but an expert scholar” (“Laureates and Beggars,” p. 708).

52
gloses. Glossing was an important part of medieval biblical exegesis: the interpretation of the Bible. The word ‘gloss’ can refer to both a marginal annotation in a manuscript, such as a translation or brief explanation of a word used in a text, or to a commentary on a text as a whole. Ashby here probably means the latter, possibly the immensely popular Glossa Ordinaria (Standard Gloss), a collection of authoritative biblical commentaries.

55
as thei before. That is, the triumvirate of Chaucer, Gower, and Lydgate invoked at the start of the poem.

59
Any creatures to my konnyng. Just as the extensive humility topos in these stanzas is a strategy to avoid blame for the politically sensitive content of the poem, so too Ashby tries to protect himself by claiming he does not want to displease anyone he knows. However, Ashby does not identify exactly who these “creatures to my konnyng” whom he does not want to offend are.

65
mony yeres of foure score. In compound numbers, “score” means twenty, so Ashby here reveals his age to be eighty (four times twenty). At this age, Ashby would have been considered to be in the final stage of his life. Classifications of the “ages of man” were popular in medieval philosophical and medical texts. The last stage of life, starting between sixty and seventy years old, was usually seen as a stage of decline and diminution. For a study on the medieval concepts of the stages of life, see Burrow, The Ages of Man.

87
faders and moders of recorde. The question of the inheritance of the throne through the male line (i.e., from father to son only) or through the general line (i.e., from either father or mother to son) was a central concern during the struggle between the houses of York and Lancaster. Both families traced their claim to the throne back to King Edward III — the Lancastrians through the male line of Edward III’s fourth son, John of Gaunt, and his son Henry IV, the grandfather of Henry VI, while the Yorkists claimed primacy through the general line of Edward III’s third son Lionel and his daughter Phillipa, the great-grandmother of Duke Richard of York. The problem with preferring the male line over the general line was that the English claim to the French throne, one of the leading causes of the Hundred Years’ War, was based on Edward III’s descent through the general line via his mother Isabella of France. Ashby here seems to claim Edward of Lancaster’s descent to both “roiaulmes” (line 89) on his paternal as well as his maternal line.

105
vilipended. The Active Policy and Dicta is the first attested use of this word, which is derived from Latin vilipendere: to consider worthless (OED, vilipend (v.)).

114
In all vertuous disposicion. The education of a future king was always an important responsibility, and even more so in the case of Prince Edward of Lancaster, on whose princely competencies the hopes of the Lancastrian cause depended after the failure of his father to retain the crown. The portrayal of Edward’s proper education was therefore an important component of Lancastrian “propaganda” in the years leading up to the Lancastrian return to England in the late 1460s. Mirrors for princes like the Active Policy and Dicta constituted an important part of the outward visibility of his royal education. In addition to writing this princely advice text, as Sobecki suggests, Ashby might have been personally involved in the early education of Prince Edward by teaching him to write (Sobecki-Words, p. 187).

119
oure althre wele. Especially towards the later Middle Ages, the central duty of the king was seen to be the protection of the common good. References to “commonwealth” and “common good” are increasingly prevalent in writings of this time, from literature to parliamentary records. The concepts occupied a central position in the criticisms of Henry VI’s rule from both the Jack Cade Rebels and the Duke of York in the years leading up to the Wars of the Roses. For instance, the Cade rebels lamented that “the commyn p[rofette] w[as] sore hurte and decresed” (Marx, ed., An English Chronicle, p. 67), a narrative that was adopted by the Duke of York in his opposition to Lancastrian policy. In response, the Lancastrian tract Somniun Vigilantis, in an attempt to restore royal authority, claims that “amonge many thinges by the whiche the commone welthe [. . .] stondyth the most principall is this, a due subjeccion [. . .] to the soverain in the sayd royame” (Gilson, ed., “A Defense of the Proscription of the Yorkists,” p. 518). For a discussion of the development of the common good as a political concept, see also Watts, Henry VI, pp. 13–80.

127–29
Of tyme passed . . . ende dothe lede. A staple of the medieval mirrors for princes and other moral or political didactic texts is the use of exempla — biblical, mythological, or more recent historical stories — to illustrate a certain moral lesson. Compare, among others, Geoffrey Chaucer’s Tale of Melibee, John Gower’s Confessio Amantis, John Lydgate’s Fall of Princes, and Thomas Hoccleve’s Regiment of Princes. Such exempla are, however, conspicuously absent from the Active Policy and Dicta.

140
He endithe not wele that wykkidly dothe. Proverbial. See Whiting E91.

143
Bothe of this England and of Fraunce. Ashby once more stresses Edward of Lancaster’s claim to both the English and the French thrones. Compare to lines 85–89.

167
covetous. Over the course of the following stanzas, which concern the recent events of Henry VI’s reign, Ashby repeatedly warns against trusting covetous people, who, because they are only concerned with their own material welfare, undermine the common good of the realm. This is in fact a concern that was first raised in the 1450s by the Duke of York and his supporters, who claimed that the king was led astray by covetous advisors who were only interested in enriching themselves. See also Watts, Henry VI, pp. 41–42 for the role of covetousness and financial security in the political thinking of both Ashby and John Fortescue.

169
in late daies. Ashby here turns explicitly to a discussion of recent events. The following stanzas are rather more critical of Henry VI’s rule than might be expected of a Lancastrian text.

193
grete batellis. The 1450s were marked by a series of battles, from minor skirmishes such as the First Battle of St Albans (1455) to large-scale clashes such as the Battle of Towton (1461). The latter, as T. L. Sutherland and A. Schmidt state in their archeological survey of the Towton battlefield, was the “largest battle ever fought on British soil” (“Battlefields,” p. 15). The Paston Letters (written 1422–1509) give close insight into the impact of the civil war on the lives of people living in England at the time.

210
polletike. “Polletike” or “politique” (MED, politik(e (adj.), sense 1a is defined as “pertaining to or concerning the spiritual or secular governance of a country or people”) was a relatively new concept in fifteenth-century political discourse. According to Paul Strohm, it represents a new type of political behavior that is aimed at political calculation and the personal advantage of the prince. All quotations of texts using this word in the MED are in fact from the fifteenth century. See Strohm, Politique.

236
Either in preisyng, either in blamyng. Mirrors for princes, by including stories of the rise and fall of previous kings, implicitly warn their royal readers that their lives and deeds, too, will be read in turn by their successors. See also Perkins, “Representing Advice in Lydgate,” p. 175.

274
live of youre own properté. Lancastrian financial policies were particularly prone to criticism, as Richard II’s lavish expenditure was one of the main points of criticism by Henry IV before his usurpation. See Nuttall, The Creation of Lancastrian Kingship, pp. 77–78.

282
Not biddynge youre counsail do al thing. Giving and receiving counsel was a vital component of the late medieval English political system. If a king’s task was to unite his subjects’ disparate interests into a coherent policy to advance the common good, he needed to rely on the information and advice given to him by his subjects. The King’s Council was the official venue for royal advice, but there were many informal channels for counsel within the royal household. The perceived primacy of counsel-taking to the proper governance of England is emphasized in the central role of this concept in political writing from the Wars of the Roses. Both the Duke of York and the Jack Cade rebels complained that the king did not admit the counsel of those who should advise him (i.e., York and his associates), and instead was led astray by self-interested counselors (i.e., Suffolk and Somerset, among others). Compare to line 2058; see also the note to that line, below.

288–95
Principally I wolde . . . avoide every smert. This stanza is eight lines, instead of the usual seven lines of Ashby’s rhyme royal.

note.p: Plato. Plato (ca. 427–347 BCE) was a Greek philosopher, student of Socrates and tutor to Aristotle. Neoplatonism, a philosophy developed in Late Antiquity on the basis of Plato’s teachings, exercised a profound influence on early Christian theology, and continued to do so throughout the Middle Ages. Most of Plato’s texts, though preserved and read by Arabic scholars, were unavailable in the Christian world until the twelfth century, when they were translated into Latin. The Liber is an entirely apocryphal text, and while it attributes many sayings to Plato none of them are based on Plato’s actual work.

div.note:
296
paie youre men. Payment of civil and royal servants was frequently late. This was a problem that was not unique to Ashby’s time of writing — Thomas Hoccleve in his Regiment of Princes, one of Ashby’s major influences, in fact frames his princely advice text as a supplication to the future Henry V to pay him his wages. Ashby also seems to have had personal experience with delayed payments. A letter sent ca. 1447 on behalf of Queen Margaret requests a payment to be made to Ashby “of his wages deue unto him by the Duc of Gloucester,” in whose household Ashby was employed before he was transferred to the Signet Office. See Maurer and Cron, Letters of Margaret, pp. 140–43.

330
unthé. The Active Policy and Dicta is the only attested use of this word in this sense (MED, unthen (v.), sense 1). See also lines 1700, 1969.

note.p: Pitagoras. Pythagoras (ca. 570–495 BCE) was a Greek philosopher and scientist. Though there are no surviving written works by Pythagoras, medieval theologians considered him one of the great ancient philosophers and the founding father of the art of mathematics. The Liber is an entirely apocryphal text, and while it attributes many sayings to Pythagoras none of them are based on his actual work.

div.note:
332
tiranship. Compare Book 8 of John of Salisbury’s Policraticus (ed. Nederman, pp. 181–231), which includes his discussion of tyranny and tyrannicide. According to his influential theory, a tyrant was not a true king, because a true king would not betray his people and undermine the common good. According to this reasoning, it would be lawful to depose a tyrant.

note.p: Hermes. The Liber’s Hermes is a conflation of the Greek god of the same name, and Hermes Trismegistus, a mythical great philosopher. The opening lines of Hermes’s section in the Liber also identify him as Enoch, an Old Testament prophet. The conflation of these three people dates back to the early Middle Ages. The Liber is an entirely apocryphal text, and while it attributes many sayings to Hermes none of them are based on existing work by a philosopher of this name. See also Sutton, p. 118n1–2.

div.note:
354
Kepe secretnesse as a secretarye. As Sobecki has noted before, secrecy is a prominent theme in the Active Policy and Dicta (Sobecki-Words, pp. 189–90). The connection between secrecy and the services of the Signet Office is reinforced by Ashby’s references to the Secretary in this line, who was the Keeper of the signet seal and the head of the office. The title of Secretary is connected to the term secretum sigillum, the secret seal, which was for a long time a synonym for signet seal, referring to any personal seal of the king or a lord, until the Signet Office became an official government office in the late fourteenth century. See also Otway-Ruthven, pp. 19–20.

392
cronicles. A popular genre of writing in the Middle Ages, chronicles were long, narrative accounts of past events, usually written in prose, often starting at Creation and leading up to the chronicler’s present time. For most of the period, chronicles were mostly produced at monasteries, though towards the later Middle Ages, cities and families also commissioned chronicles. Chronicles often have a strong regional or political bias. Many of the surviving chronicles contemporary with the Active Policy and Dicta are written from a Yorkist perspective, such as Marx, ed., An English Chronicle. In this line, Ashby encourages Edward to read chronicles as a source of knowledge about past events, specifically to discover which regions are prone to rebellion — such as Kent, the main locus of both Jack Cade’s rebellion (1450) and the Great Rising (or Peasants’ Revolt, 1381).

403
Thurgh the fals devel to theim conveiede. The syntax makes this line somewhat confusing: the sense probably is “even though the fals devil directed them,” omitting the proposition “to.”

408
Be wele ware of falsehode in felawship. Proverbial. See Whiting F45.

419
Pretendyng right to youre coronacion. That is, the Yorkists, who claimed the English crown for themselves based on their descent from Edward III through the general line (see note to line 87, above).

427–28
And be ye . . . to be reviled. Perhaps this is a reference to Henry VI’s attempt to enforce a reconciliation between Duke Richard of York and Queen Margaret on Loveday 1458. See the Introduction, p. 7.

436
The trouthe is not hid. Proverbial. See Whiting S490.

467
a Secretarie. Compare to line 354. The Secretary, as the head of the Signet Office, is here singled out as equally important to the king’s welfare as those who are charged with the health of the king’s body (a doctor) and soul (a confessor).

479
Bothe knyghtes, squiers, clercs, and yomen. Ashby here lists a few prominent social groups from late medieval society. Knights were traditionally mounted warriors, though in the later Middle Ages they mainly fulfilled administrative tasks in their local communicaties rather than rendering military service. Squires were attendants to knights, often those aspiring to become knights at a later stage in their lives. Yeomen were landholding farmers. The term “clerk,” from Latin clericus, originally referred to a member of the clergy: someone in religious orders. Towards the later Middle Ages, the meaning was gradually widened to refer to someone who is educated, and eventually an officer in charge of writing or keeping accounts.

492–93
A peny spent . . . Availith two. Proverbial. See Whiting P125.

499
Provide that your communes may be welthy. Ashby presents a financial interpretation of the common good, in which the welfare of the people is only expressed in monetary terms, rather than moral, judicial, or physical. It is a conception of the common good that corresponds to what Ashby views as the foremost danger to political stability: “covetise.” See also the note to line 167, above.

514
poverté departithe felaship. Proverbial. See Whiting P334.

527
bryng up ayen clothe makyng. John Scattergood has suggested that these lines are a reference to legislation passed in 1463 to support the clothmaking industry, following a petition by the commons to that same effect (“Date and Composition,” pp. 168–69). However, with the more likely dating of the Active Policy and Dicta in 1461–1462 (see the Introduction, p. 15), this seems not to be a reference to the statute passed by Edward IV but rather, perhaps, to concerns on the failing clothmaking industry that were already present before the legislation was passed the following year.

540
statute of youre progenitours. The famous Statute of Labourers from 1351 was meant to regulate labor after the devastating mortality rates of the Black Death, setting a maximum wage for workmen. However, Ashby probably refers to another statute here, enacted by Edward III in 1363, which regulates the clothing for different strata of society (Luders, ed., Statutes of the Realm, 1:380–82). See also Scattergood, “Date and Composition,” pp. 169–71.

548
shuld nat yeve clothyng. Late medieval lords often gave their servants and retainers livery, clothing that through their colors or heraldic signs identified that person as part of the lord’s affinity: his social and political network. A powerful lord’s livery would signify that the wearer was under that nobleman’s protection. As the practice of providing livery grew in the fourteenth century, so too did concerns over this practice. Some abused their privileged position of being in the favor and under the protection of a powerful lord by extorting the local population. From the late fourteenth century onwards, the commons repeatedly asked for legislation to curb the granting of livery. See Chapter 11, “Livery,” in Rose, Maintenance in Medieval England, pp. 268–315.

552
maintenance. “Maintenance” (“wrongful or officious interference in others’ law suits; support, backing; abetting a wrong or wrong-doer,” MED, maintenaunce (n.), senses 1a, 2a, and 2b) could refer to a range of abuses of the legal system, but most often meant the interference of a powerful lord in a lawsuit in order to support a litigant who was under his protection. Concerns about maintenance were therefore often related to the practice of the giving of livery, which signified a lord’s favor to the wearer (see note to line 548, above). See Rose, Maintenance in Medieval England.

555
Every man ought to lyve undere a lawe. Compare John Fortescue’s theory of the kingdom ruled by a king bound by law, the dominium politicum et regale in In Praise of the Laws of England, Chapter 13: “So a people that wills to erect itself into a kingdom or any other body politic must always set up one man for the government of all that body [. . .] The law, indeed, by which a group of men is made into a people, resembles the sinews of the physical body, for, just as the body is held together by the sinews, so this body mystical is bound together and preserved as one by the law” (Fortescue, In Praise of the Laws of England, ed. Lockwood, pp. 20–21).

570
To use the bowe and shetyng for disport. The fourteenth and fifteenth centuries saw several statutes and laws that obliged English men to practice archery on Sundays and holidays, which, due its obvious military value, was seen as a more useful pursuit than other pastimes and sports. See, for instance, the king’s proclamation to the sheriff of Kent from 1363, recorded in the Calendar of Close Rolls, which explicitly outlines the usefulness of this pastime for the king and the kingdom: “every able bodied man on feast days when he has leisure shall in his sports use bows and arrows, pellets or bolts, and shall learn and practise the art of shooting, forbidding all and singular on pain of imprisonment to attend or meddle with hurling of stones, loggats, or quoits, handball, football, club ball, cambuc, cock fighting or other vain games of no value; as the people of the realm, noble and simple, used heretofore to practise the said art in their sports, whence by God’s help came forth honour to the kingdom and advantage to the king in his actions of war, and now the said art is almost wholly disused, and the people indulge in the games aforesaid and other dishonest and unthrifty games, whereby the realm is like to be kept without archers” (CCR, Edward III, 11:534–35).

577
Billes of compleint. A bill of complaint or petition submitted by a person to the Chancellor or the king would often be the starting point of a lawsuit. It outlines the offences that were committed against the litigant, and by whom, as well as a plea for justice. See also MED, bille (n.), sense 2a.

581
frivolly. This line is the only attested use of the adverb “frivolly” in Middle English, according to the MED (frivolli (adv.)). The adjectival form, “frivol” or “frivolous,” derived from French frivole or Latin frivolus is more common, especially in the post-medieval period (OED, frivol (adj. & n.), frivolous (adj.)).

615
Aftur the oolde dogge, the yonge whelpe barkes. Proverbial. See Whiting D298.

652
obeiceantly. The use of “obeiceantly” in this line is uncommon. The MED, obeisauntli (adv.), sense 1b gives for this particular use of the word, only attested in the Active Policy, the following suggestion: “?in a manner which exacts obedience; ?in obedience to law or custom.” The latter sense seems more appropriate, referring to a manner of ruling based on law and learning as opposed to the rule of “litle discrecion” (line 650) by someone who is not learned.

note.p: Satis cito . . . bene sit. Ashby assigns no source to this Latin passage.

div.note:
667–68
Oure nature desirith . . . us with governance. Compare John Fortescue’s description of the origin of the dominium politicum et regale (see also note to line 555, above), in In Praise of the Laws of England, ed. Lockwood, Chapter 13.

673
conjectour. The common meaning of “conjectour” is “soothsayer.” The MED lists the meaning of “schemer” only for this particular line in the Active Policy and Dicta (see MED, conjectere, -our (n.), sense 1b).

note.p: Socrates. Socrates (ca. 470–399 BCE) was a Greek philosopher. He authored no works himself, and the main source for his philosophy are the dialogues written by his student Plato. Socrates continued to be a well-known name in the medieval Christian world, though his philosophy was little known. The Liber is an entirely apocryphal text, and while it attributes many sayings to Socrates none of them are based on his actual teachings.

div.note:
695
lawe positife. Positive law is man-made law, formally decreed through statutes and legislation. The word derives from the Latin ponere (participle positus): “to place, to ordain.” The counterpart of such man-made law is the natural law, a system of law supposedly innate to humankind. Though originating in classical writings, the notion of the natural law in the Middle Ages was discussed in detail by Albertus Magnus and in particular by Thomas Aquinas in his influential Summa Theologica. Largely overlapping with the precepts of natural law, a third system of law distinguished by medieval writers was divine law, the body of rules decreed by God (see lines 238–41). Ashby here summarizes the natural law as “do to others as you would like others to do to you,” the golden rule common to many religions that is often repeated in the Bible.

726
withoute resumyng. Among the more unpopular policies of Henry VI were his series of resumptions of grants, in particular his Act of Resumption in 1450. This meant that the Crown took back into possession lands or titles that had previously been granted to persons or institutions, in an attempt to improve royal finances.

730–34
A man to . . . be suche takyng. Ashby speaks from experience: his own office of Constable of Dynevor was annulled as part of the 1450 Act of Resumption.

770
He that is warned is not deceived. Proverbial. See Whiting W49.

773
And the comyn wele of this region. The common good or commonweal became an increasingly important political concept in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, with royal policy being judged by its effect on the welfare of the kingdom and the common people. It is this discourse that the Duke of York most successfully employed in his attempts to justify his resistance against royal government. See for instance Watts, “Ideas, Principles and Politics,” pp. 121–22 and Ormrod, “‘Common Profit.’”

807
temporal lorde. A temporal lord is a secular lord, as opposed to a spiritual lord, a bishop or abbot. Throughout most of the Middle Ages, powerful political officials, such as the Chancellor and the Treasurer, were almost always clergymen, though this practice began to change towards the end of the medieval period. The fifteenth century saw a remarkable increase in the number of lay appointments to the office of Treasurer, though the position of Chancellor remained more conservatively in the hands of churchmen. The only exceptions in Ashby’s lifetime were the brief appointment of Thomas Beaufort in 1410–1412, and that of Richard Neville (the Yorkist supporter known as the “Kingmaker”) by Duke Richard of York during his Protectorate in 1455–1456.

note.p: Gregorius. Gregory the Great (ca. 540–604 CE) was one of the four Church Fathers (along with Augustine, Ambrose, and Jerome), early theologians whose writings, in addition to the Bible, formed the basis of Christian doctrine. The Liber is an entirely apocryphal text, and while it attributes many sayings to Gregory none of them are based on his actual work.

div.note:
824–25
And your matiers . . . to goode endyng. Proverbial. See Whiting B204. These lines are echoed later in 966–67 and 2020.

837
nat worthe two russhes. Proverbial. See Whiting R250.

note.p: Omerus. Homer (8th century BCE) was a Greek poet, credited as the author of the Iliad and the Odyssey. While Homer’s works were not available in the medieval Christian world, the epic story of the fall of Troy was transmitted through many other texts and remained hugely popular throughout the Middle Ages. Ashby’s near contemporary John Lydgate, to name just one example, wrote the epic poem Troy Book which runs to over 30,000 lines. It is worth repeating that the Liber is an entirely apocryphal text, and while it attributes many sayings to Homer none of them are based on his actual work.

div.note:
849
Retoriq and musyk. Medieval education was divided into seven fields deemed to be important to every well-educated person: the trivium (consisting of rhetoric, grammar, and logic) and the quadrivium (consisting of music, astronomy, geometry, and arithmetic).

857
flatering speche. Compare Hoccleve, Regiment of Princes, ed. Blyth, lines 3039–66 and 5253–85. Hoccleve portrays flattery, personified as Favel, as one of the most pressing dangers to the king. Flatterers cannot be trusted to tell the king the truth, because they are only concerned with pleasing him. Compared to Hoccleve, Ashby pays very little attention to the dangers of flattery, focusing instead on the more overt self-interestedness of “covetise.”

870
Put no ful truste in the comonalté. Ashby’s is the earliest of two recorded usages of this proverb in Whiting, C391, though the essence of the saying is very similar to the more commonly cited proverb C392: “In the Commons no man may trust,” in use from the late fourteenth century.

871
Thai be ever wavering in variance. Despite Ashby’s insistence that the king should keep the commons happy, he evidently does not view them as trustworthy political partners. As described in the Introduction (pp. 5–8), it was the Yorkist faction that enjoyed the most widespread public support. Consequently, some Lancastrian texts downplay the value of public opinion in political matters. Ashby’s condemnation of the unreliability of the common people is mirrored in the Lancastrian polemical tract Somnium Vigilantis (Dream of the Watchful One), which argues that public support is no legitimate basis for political authority, because the people’s allegiance may change at any moment. See Gilson, ed., “A Defence of the Proscription of the Yorkists,” for the original text.

898–99
Saint Petur saithe . . . goode or unworthy. Saint Peter was one of the Twelve Apostles of Christ and he was regarded as the first pope (Bishop of Rome). The Bible contains two books that were believed to be written by St. Peter: the First Epistle (1 Peter) and Second Epistle (2 Peter). The reference here is to 1 Peter 2:13–14: “Be ye subject therefore to every human creature for God’s sake: whether it be to the king as excelling; Or to governors as sent by him for the punishment of evildoers, and for the praise of the good” (Douay-Rheims Bible).

note.p: Aristotiles. Aristotle (384–322 BCE) was a Greek philosopher. His works became particularly influential on Christian philosophy after they were translated from Arabic or Greek into Latin in the twelfth century. The Liber is an entirely apocryphal text, and while it attributes many sayings to Aristotle none of them are based on his actual work. In additon, this is a misattributed quote: in the Liber, it is part of Pitagoras’s section (Franceschini, p. 430).

Zelon. Solon (ca. 630–560 BCE) was an Athenian law reformer and political philosopher. His writings, which include some poetry, survive only in fragments. The Liber is an entirely apocryphal text, and while it attributes many sayings to Solon none of them are based on his actual work.

div.note:
926–27
Truste nat oonly . . . in comon clamour. These lines are not in the Latin passage on which Ashby bases this stanza. As his own addition, it draws attention to the perceived unreliability of the common people and popular opinion by the Lancastrians; the Yorkists, after all, were the ones who enjoyed the most popular support. See also the note to line 870, above.

932
With lawe. Compare to Sir John Fortescue’s theory of the dominium politicum et regale, in Chapter 13 of In Praise of the Laws of England (see above, note to line 555).

note.p: Plato. This is a partly misattributed quote. In the Liber, this advice appears in the section on King Alexander (see note to line 1925, below), as the answers of Plato and Aristotle to Alexander’s questions. The first part (“decet rem . . . perficere cognatum”) is attributed to Plato, and the second part (“qui servos habet . . . procuratorem constituas”) is attributed to Aristotle (Franceschini, pp. 527–28).

div.note:
947–48
Th’age of man . . . shewith not madnesse. In opening this stanza with the juxtaposition between a person’s age and his character, rather than the Latin statement that “to govern a people is not fit for a boy,” Ashby perhaps draws attention to the differences between the “old” Henry VI and the young Prince Edward. In claiming that age does not equal competence, these lines advocate Prince Edward’s suitability for the royal office in contrast to his older father, who has proven to be an inadequate king.

973
The ende shall showe every thinge as it is. Proverbial. See Whiting E81.

note.p: Aristotiles. This quote does not appear in the Liber. Bühler, though admitting he did not find the source for this stanza, suggests that it may be an adaptation from Aristotle’s Nicomachean Ethics (“The Liber de Dictis,” p. 283n7).

div.note:
1051
This they shall obey youre highnesse most best. This stanza draws attention to the king’s central task of protecting the common good, though not as the raison d’être for a king but rather as a precaution to protect his own position. It is typical for Ashby’s political theory that the moral aspects of kingship are a means to achieve political stability rather than an end in themselves.

note.p: Hermes. Misattributed quote. In the Liber this is part of the section on Sedechias (Franceschini, pp. 400–01). The identity of Sedechias is obscure. Despite the similarity in their names, he should not be identified as the biblical King Zedekiah, who was not particularly known for his wisdom. Sutton notes that Margaret Schofield, in her 1936 edition of Scrope’s Dicts and Sayings, suggests that he might be identified as Seth, the third son of Adam and Eve (p. 117n1).

Loginon. The Liber identifies Loginon as a man who was born in Ethiopia in the time of David the Prophet (the biblical King David, ca. 10th–9th century BCE). He is known in Arabic wisdom literature as Luqman, a wise man after whom one of the chapters of the Qur’an was named. The Liber is an entirely apocryphal text, and while it attributes sayings to Loginon none of them are based on his actual work.

Omerus. Misattributed quote. This quote is actually not taken from the Liber, but from the Bible: “ex abundantia enim cordis os loquitur” (out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh, Matthew 12:34, Douay-Rheims translation).
Socrates. Misattributed quote. In the Liber, this quote is attributed to Homer (Franceschini, p. 418).

div.note:
1086
man polletyke. See the note to line 210, above.

1090
Bi his wiffe. Discussions of gender are remarkably absent from Ashby’s work, despite his employment as Queen Margaret’s signet clerk for more than fifteen years prior to the Lancastrian family’s exile. This is one of the few exceptions (see also lines 1611–14 and 2064–66). This line does not seem sympathetic to women’s influence in politics, but it can also be read as a condemnation of Henry VI’s weak politics, which necessitated Margaret to take an active role in government.

note.p: Hermes. Misattributed quote. In the Liber, this quote is attributed to Tac (or Zac) (Franceschini, p. 416). As Sutton notes, Tac or Zac might refer to the Egyptian god Thoth, and the short section attributed to this philosopher “seems to be a coda to the Hermes chapter, for Zac too deals mainly with the issue of good kingship” (p. 121n3.1).

div.note:
1101–02
To dissimile . . . some herd distresse. Ashby seems to suggest here that, in certain dangerous circumstances, it may be justifiable to lie or conceal the truth. It is one of the many pieces of advice in the Active Policy and Dicta that is not in line with the traditional view of the morally just king, but rather seems to suggest a new type of vigilant kingship emerging in the fifteenth century (discussed in Strohm, Politique; see also the note to lines 1325–31, below). It is characteristic of Ashby that this controversial statement is immediately followed by lines that encourage the exact opposite: to be open and honest.

note.p: Aristotiles. Misattributed quote. In the Liber, this quote is attributed to Hermes (Franceschini, p. 411).
Hermes. Misattributed quote. In the Liber, this quote is attributed to Tac (Franceschini, p. 415 and p. 415n5).
Hermes. Misattributed quote. In the Liber, this quote is attributed to Tac (Franceschini, p. 416).
Aristotiles. Misattributed quote. In the Liber, this quote is attributed to Socrates (Franceschini, p. 447).
Aristotiles. Misattributed quote. In the Liber, this quote is attributed to Socrates (Franceschini, p. 448).

div.note:
1152
That he knewe before his regne. Aside from being a general piece of advice about whom to trust, these lines also reflect on Ashby’s own trustworthiness as an old servant who knew Prince Edward before he became king.

1155
To glose hym, to please hym. Compare lines 856–60 on the dangers of flattery, as well as Hoccleve, Regiment of Princes, ed. Blyth, lines 3039–66 and 5253–85. See also the note to lines 857, above.

1169–70
He that can . . . folkes therin lerne. A variation on a proverb included in Whiting’s collection, taken from other translations of the Dicts and Sayings tradition (see Introduction, “Sources for The Active Policy and Dicta,” pp. 20–23). See Whiting G407.

1200
Wisedam. Of all the virtues necessary for a king to have, wisdom is the most prominent in the Active Policy and Dicta. As one of the four cardinal virtues — prudence (wisdom), justice, fortitude, and temperance — it occupied an important place in any princely advice text, but Ashby even views it as the source of all other virtues.

note.p: Hermes. Misattributed quote. In the Liber, this quote is attributed to Sedechias (Franceschini, p. 400).

Res que est . . . forciores suo fine. The exact meaning of the Latin is unclear here. Ashby does not translate these lines in the following stanza. His seven lines of Middle English verse are entirely based on the first half of the Latin quotation in this paragraph. The Liber provides no further context to this statement, and the translator of the Middle English prose Dicts and Sayings omits this sentence from the texts (Sutton, p. 12. Plato, lines 364–65). Perhaps there is a thematic echo in lines 2016–19 of the Active Policy and Dicta, below: “The begynnyng of goodenesse is bittyr, / The ende is right swete of natural kynde; / The begynnyng of shreudnesse is swetter, / But the ende is of bitternesse the gretter,” although these lines are preceded by a different Latin passage of the same meaning.

div.note:
1241
Repute never oon enemye litel. This line is cited in Whiting as a variation on the common proverb, “there is no little enemy” (E99).

1311
Suche as the kyng is, suche bene al other. Proverbial. See Whiting K56.

note.p: Hermes. Misattributed quote. In the Liber, this quote is attributed to Sedechias (Franceschini, p. 399).

div.note:
1325–31
Yf a king . . . thinges in assurance. This idea that the king should always be vigilant and expect opposition to his rule from every corner is one of the reasons why Ashby’s text has been cited as an example of a new type of kingship that is more concerned with protecting the king’s position than with the common good. See Watts, Henry VI, p. 43.

note.p: Hermes. Misattributed quote. In the Liber, this quote is attributed to Sedechias (Franceschini, p. 399).
Hermes. Misattributed quote. In the Liber, this quote is attributed to Sedechias (Franceschini, p. 399).

div.note:
1344–45
For of a . . . grete fyre / Comyth. Proverbial. See Whiting S559.

1341–45
As a litil . . . many a sire. Ashby’s use of the illness metaphor calls to mind the familiar medieval concept of the body politic: a political theory that envisioned the kingdom as a body, with the king as its head. This image, popularized by John of Salisbury’s Policraticus, is used throughout later medieval political writings, including by John Fortescue in In Praise of the Laws of England (see the note to line 555, above). Though Ashby does not employ this concept in his poem, the influence of the kingdom as a body can be seen in these lines.

note.p: Hermes. Misattributed quote. In the Liber, this quote is attributed to Sedechias (Franceschini, p. 400).

div.note:
1350
huntyng. Hunting was the quintessential aristocratic leisure activity in medieval England. It formed an important part of the chivalric ethos — even the pursuit of an unattainable lady, in the literary courtly love tradition, came to be symbolized as a hunt. Hunting was both a mark of social status and formed part of aristocratic education of young men. Ashby does not urge the prince to give up hunting entirely, but to practice moderation.

1352
ornatly. This is the only attested use of this word for the Middle English period (MED, ornatli (adv.)), and the earliest attested use in the OED (OED, ornately (adv.)).

note.p: Hermes. Misattributed quote. In the Liber, this quote is attributed to Sedechias (Franceschini, p. 400).
Hermes. Misattributed quote. In the Liber, this quote is attributed to Sedechias (Franceschini, p. 400).
Hermes. Misattributed quote. In the Liber, this quote is attributed to Sedechias (Franceschini, p. 400).
Hermes. Misattributed quote. In the Liber, this quote is attributed to Sedechias (Franceschini, p. 401).

In multum . . . non expendas. Ashby does not provide a source for this quote. It is in fact taken from the final section of the Liber, titled Sapientium Dicta (Sayings of the Wise Ones), a collection of diverse other philosophers. In the Liber, this quote is preceded by the phrase “et dixit alter” (and another one says) (Franceschini, p. 587).

div.note:
1401
Hec Ovidius. The final words “Hec Ovidius” suggest that these lines were based on a quotation by Ovid, but Ashby does not precede this stanza with a Latin passage. Ovid (ca. 43 BCE–17 CE) was a Roman poet, whose best known works are Metamorphoses and The Art of Love. His poetry was very influential in the Middle Ages. To name just one example, Chaucer adapts the Ovidian story of Ceyx and Alcione in the opening section of his Book of the Duchess. It is unclear why Ashby refers to him here — he does not quote a Latin source, and Ovid is not one of the philosophers included in the Liber.

1407
The tonge breketh boon, thaugh he be tendre. Proverbial. See Whiting T384.

1418
douce. The gloss “sweet” here is for the French word “douce.”

1422
As the kyng is, suche bene al in his cure. See the note to line 1311, above.

note.p: Assaron. It is unknown whom this name refers to. In contrast to most other sections of the Liber, Asseron’s chapter does not start with any biographical information on the philosopher in question. Sutton notes Michael Livingston’s suggestion that Asseron might refer to Fatima Az-Zahra, Mohammed’s daughter (Sutton, p. 138n16.1). In addition, this is a misattributed quote: in the Liber, this quote is attributed to Ptolemy (Franceschini, p. 534).

Ypocras. Hippocrates (ca. 460–370 BCE) was a Greek physician and philosopher who is remembered as the founding father of the field of medicine. His writings and that of his followers, often attributed to him, remained popular throughout the Middle Ages. The Liber is an entirely apocryphal text, and while it attributes sayings to Hippocrates none of them are based on his actual work.

div.note:
1463–64
he that dothe . . . reason, and skyle. These lines are cited in Whiting as a variation of the common proverb, “do well and have well” (D278).

1466
nygonship. This is the only attested use of this word, according to both the MED (nigounshipe (n.)) and OED (nigonship (n.)). It is derived from the noun nigoun, “miser,” which is itself an uncommon variant of the more commonly used noun niggard (OED, nigon (n.)).

1465–70
Be nat in . . . spryng and florissh. This stanza is only six lines, instead of the usual seven lines of Ashby’s rhyme royal.

note.p: Diogenes. Diogenes (ca. 413–324 BCE) was a Greek philosopher who is best remembered for his asceticism, spending most of his life living in self-imposed poverty. None of his written works survive. The Liber is an entirely apocryphal text, and while it attributes sayings to Diogenes none of them are based on his actual work.

div.note:
1478
A freende is knowen in necessité. Whiting cites this line as one of the many variations of the proverb, “a friend in need” (F634).

1484
natural bloode. This is an uncommon phrase in Middle English, usually used in a medical context to refer to the four humors (the theory that the body was composed of four bodily fluids — blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile — which influenced a person’s character and mood). In this case, however, it seems more likely that Ashby combines two secondary meanings of both “natural” and “blood”: “natural” in the sense of “hereditary, by birth; by blood, (one’s) own” (MED, natural (adj.), senses 5a and 6b), and “blood” in the sense of “lineage, descent, ancestry; relationship by birth, blood relationship, consanguinity, kinship” (MED, blod (n.1), senses 6a and 6b). It fits with Ashby’s general distrust of other people’s intentions that he here seems to suggest that only family members are to be trusted.

1499–1505
A kyng shulde . . . your enemyes grace. Who to trust is an important theme in Ashby’s advice, especially with reference to whose counsel should be adopted. The long list of untrustworthy persons in this stanza is hardly comforting. At various points, Ashby has already pointed out that the common people cannot be trusted either (see lines 870–71 and 926–27). In general, those who can be trusted are wise, old men — not coincidentally, a description that includes Ashby himself.

1514
his counseil have of hym governance. One of the big questions of Henry VI’s reign concerns the power balance between the king and his Council. Because Henry VI became king at only nine months old, for years the kingdom was ruled by the King’s Council. Historians disagree over the extent to which Henry VI took active rule after he came of age. A detailed discussion of the contemporary evidence is presented by Watts in Henry VI. Compare this stanza also to the following stanza.

note.p: Salamon. Solomon (ca. 10th century BCE) appears in the Old Testament as King of Israel. He was revered for his wisdom, held up as an example to medieval monarchs. The Liber is an entirely apocryphal text, and while it attributes sayings to Solomon none of them are based on his actual teachings. This is a misattributed quote: it does not appear in the Liber, but comes from the Rule of St. Benedict, which Ashby may have encountered in collections of aphorisms (florilegia): “Omnia fac cum consilio et post factum non paeniteberis” (do everything with counsel, and afterwards you will not repent) (Vogüé and Neufville, eds., Règle de Saint Benoît, p. 454).

div.note:
1555
werkys of mercy. The Seven Works of Mercy were an important part of medieval lay piety, instructing the faithful to perform the following seven charitable acts: feed the hungry, give drink to the thirsty, clothe the naked, harbor the homeless, visit the sick, ransom the imprisoned, and bury the dead.

1560–61
ye shul make . . . have made guidyng. This is a reference to the commonplace belief that upon a person’s death, they will face divine judgment of their deeds and misdeeds. In anticipation of the Last Judgment, most souls of the deceased would face some measure of punishment in hell before they would be allowed to enter heaven.

note.p: Hermes. The first part of this passage is indeed attributed to Hermes in the Liber, but the second sentence appears as a saying by Tac (Franceschini, pp. 404, 416).
Hermes. While most of this passage is indeed attributed to Hermes in the Liber, the final sentence (“Et cave a [. . .] nascitur odium”) is attributed to Zelon (Franceschini, pp. 406, 420).

div.note:
1598
this transitory world. Throughout the Active Policy and Dicta, Ashby displays an awareness of the transitory nature of all worldly power and possessions. This was a common theme in medieval writing, and one that Ashby would explore further in his prison poem, the Prisoner’s Reflections (in Mooney and Arn, eds., The Kingis Quair, pp. 153–63).

note.p: Hermes. Misattributed quote. In the Liber, this passage appears in the section titled Sapientium Dicta (Sayings of the Wise Ones), a collection of diverse other philosophers. In the Liber, this quote is attributed to Amonius, possibly Ammonius Hermiae, (ca. 440–517), a Greek Neoplatonist philosopher (see the note to ¶2, above) (Franceschini, p. 560).

div.note:
1622
nat worth a strawe. Proverbial. See Whiting S815.

1618–24
That kyng that . . . therto subget be. This stanza is again reminiscent of Fortescue’s theory of the dominium politicum et regale: of the king who is bound by the laws to serve the common good of the realm (in contrast with the dominium regale, in which the king subjects the kingdom and its subjects to his own will). See Fortescue, In Praise of the Laws of England, ed. Lockwood.

1653–58
Yeve never power . . . uppon your nekke. This stanza is only six lines, instead of the usual seven lines of Ashby’s rhyme royal.

1658
set his fote uppon your nekke. Proverbial. See Whiting F480.

1664–65
For to meche . . . be over bolde. Proverbial. See Whiting H632.

note.p: Hermes. Misattributed quote. In the Liber, this quote is attributed to Sedechias (Franceschini, pp. 400–01).

div.note:
1685
goode counseil. Compare lines 281–82; see also the note on line 282, above.

1692–93
He that can . . . it in sadnesse. Compare line 354; see also the note on that line, above, about the role of secrecy in Ashby’s political advice.

1700
unthé. See the note to line 330, above.

note.p: Enesius. It is unknown whom this name refers to. In contrast to most other sections of the Liber, Enesius’s chapter does not start with any biographical information on the philosopher in question.

Galienus. Galen (ca. 129–216) was a Greek physician and philosopher, whose medical writings remained very influential throughout the Middle Ages. He was a proponent of the medical theory of the four bodily humors: the idea that the human body consisted of four fluids (blood, pleghm, black bile, and yellow bile), which influenced a person’s mood and character. The Liber is an entirely apocryphal text, and while it attributes sayings to Galen none of them are based on his actual work.

div.note:
1729
To knowe hymself. Proverbial. See Whiting K100.

note.p: Tesilius. Tesilius’s chapter does not start with any biographical information to identify this philosopher. Sutton, based on Schofield’s suggestion that this name should be read as “Basilius,” suggests that it might refer to St. Basil, Bishop of Caesarea, a fourth-century Church Doctor (p. 139n20.1).

Maedarges. It is unknown whom this name refers to. In contrast to most other sections of the Liber, Maedargas’s chapter does not start with any biographical information on the philosopher in question. Sutton suggests that it might be St. Medardus, the sixth-century Bishop of Noyon (p. 139n19.1).

div.note:
1771–76
Yf any people . . . governe many moo. This stanza is only six lines, instead of the usual seven lines of Ashby’s rhyme royal.

note.p: Aristotiles. Misattributed quote. This passage is taken from the final section of the Liber, titled Sapientium Dicta (Sayings of the Wise Ones), a collection of diverse other philosophers. In the Liber, this quote is preceded by the phrase “et dixit alter” (and another one says) (Franceschini, p. 578).

div.note:
1784–85
Men shuld serche . . . of there governance. Compare Hoccleve’s Regiment of Princes, ed. Blyth, lines 2556–62:
O worthy Kyng benigne, Edward the laste,
Thow haddist ofte in herte a drede impressid,
Which that thyn humble goost ful sore agaste;
And to knowe if thow cursid were or blessid,
Among the peple ofte hastow thee dressid
Into contree in symple array allone
To heere what men seide of thy persone.

note.p: Aristotiles. Misattributed quote. This passage is taken from the final section of the Liber, titled Sapientium Dicta (Sayings of the Wise Ones), a collection of diverse other philosophers. In the Liber, this quote is preceded by the phrase “et dixit alter” (and another one says) (Franceschini, p. 571).
Hermes. Misattributed quote. In the Liber, this quote is attributed to Tac (Franceschini, pp. 415–16).

div.note:
1858
geason. This is the only attested use of this word as a noun in the Middle English period (MED, gesoun (adj. & n.), sense 1c).

1866
golde is pured by fire craftly. Proverbial. See Whiting G298.

1883
predacion. This is the only attested use of this word for the Middle English period (MED, predacion (n.)), and the earliest attested use in the OED (OED, predation (n.)).

1886
as a fader. In some medieval political writings, the kingdom was viewed as a minor who was therefore in need of a king to act as its father (or guardian).

note.p: Tholomeus. Ptolemy (ca. 100–170) was a Greek mathematician and astrologer, whose writings heavily influenced ideas of geography in the medieval west. The Liber is an entirely apocryphal text, and while it attributes sayings to Ptolemy none of them are based on his actual work. In addition, this is a misattributed quote. In the Liber, this quote is attributed to Alexander (see note to line 1925, below) (Franceschini, p. 531).
Tholomeus. Misattributed quote. In the Liber, this quote is attributed to Alexander (see note to line 1925, below) (Franceschini, p. 529).

div.note:
1925
kyng Alexandre, the Emperour. Alexander the Great (356–323 BCE) was an ancient Greek king who is best remembered for his military conquests, including Persia and parts of India. In the Middle Ages, Alexander was remembered as one of the Nine Worthies: great men from history and legend who represented the powerful and chivalric ideals that medieval rulers aspired to. As a young boy, Alexander was tutored by the famous philosopher Aristotle. A popular medieval didactic genre was apocryphal letters of princely advice supposedly written by Aristotle to Alexander while he was on his military campaigns.
Despite Ashby’s repeated insistence on the didactic value of stories for the education of the prince in the opening stanzas of the Active Policy (see lines 127–30, 155–57, 204–07), this is the only instance in the poem where Ashby explicitly refers to a historical example. The exemplum — a mythical or historical story to underline a certain moral or political lesson — was a central characteristic of the medieval mirror for princes and other didactic texts, as evidenced by Gower’s Confessio Amantis, Hoccleve’s Regiment of Princes, and Lydgate’s Fall of Princes, among others. Ashby’s lack of exempla is therefore a notable choice, and one that seems to distance his poem from the long tradition of advice literature.

1945–46
Who that is . . . grete and splendiferous. These lines call to mind the contemporary criticism on the Dukes of Suffolk and Somerset, Henry VI’s favorites, who were handsomely rewarded for their services to the king. Both Suffolk and Somerset were blamed by the common people and by the Yorkist party for subverting the political order because of their supposedly self-interested counsel. Fears of such reproaches are evident throughout the Active Policy and Dicta in Ashby’s repeated warnings against covetous men and selfish counsel.

1946
splendiferous. This is the only attested use of this word for the Middle English period (MED, splendiferous (adj.)), and the earliest attested use in the OED (OED, splendiferous (adj.)).

1969
unthé. See the note to line 330, above.

1971–72
For trouthe at . . . otherwhile ivyl gramed. Proverbial. See Whiting T507.

2014
wastyng water in the see. Proverbial. See Whiting W80.

note.p: Socrates. Misattributed quote. This passage does not appear in the Liber; it is unclear where Ashby took it from.

div.note:
2058
goode counseil in hym that is not herde. The idea that Henry VI did not admit the counsel of those who deserved to advise the king was a common criticism of royal policy in the 1450s and one that was repeated by both the Jack Cade rebels and Duke Richard of York. York, as a prominent peer of the realm, viewed himself as one of those who should be allowed to counsel the king, and resented the influence of Suffolk and Somerset. The fact that Ashby repeats the charge here does not necessarily mean that Ashby agreed with the Yorkist criticism, but at the very least that “counseil in hym that is not herde” was recognized as problematic.

2066
In love of women. Compare line 1090; see also the note to that line, above. Ashby heavily tones down the antifeminist message of the Latin passage on which he bases his advice, omitting the attack on women (who “prepare snares”) and turning it into a lesson on moderation instead.

note.p: Hermes. Misattributed quote. In the Liber, this quote is attributed to Sedechias (Franceschini, p. 399).

div.note:
2113–19
As it semeth . . . sowle and body. This stanza reinforces the interdependence of the king and the people, in line with many contemporary texts of political theory. Compare again Fortescue’s discussion of the origin of states in Chapter 13 of In Praise of the Laws of England (see note to line 555, above). The last line calls to mind the image of the body politic.

2129
liberalité. This is the only attested use of the word in this particular sense — the usual meaning is “generosity” (MED, liberalité (n.), sense 1b).

2140
how is it shal be blowen. Possibly a reference to the common proverb, “whenso (howsoever) the wind blows.” See Whiting W346.

2155–61
Thus ye shul . . . descripcion or jugement. Compare this stanza to Ashby’s other known poem, the Prisoner’s Reflections. Inspired by Boethius’s Consolation of Philosophy — one of the most influential texts of the Middle Ages — this prison poem teaches its readers how to patiently suffer adversity and reconcile oneself with one’s fate.

2162
delectably. This is the only attested use of the word in this particular sense (MED, delectabli (adv.), sense 1c).

2169–70
oon mouthe . . . more thanne speke. Proverbial. See Whiting E6.
